52	\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
53	\label{sec:results-differential}
54	
55	Features exhibit a continuous gradient of depth sensitivity, with a data-driven binary partition as the strongest structure: $k{=}2$ clustering in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space yields silhouette\,=\,0.632 (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}), separating \emph{drifting} features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio; $|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) from \emph{non-drifting} ones.
56	We use the shorthand \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) for this partition and further resolve a 3/1/3 characterization using domain-informed criteria: entropy std occupies a sole \emph{intermediate} position (large level shift $d{=}0.55$, low monotonicity $|\rho|{=}0.16$); the remaining three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$; CV shift $<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting).
57	This partition is robust under heteroscedasticity-corrected metrics (below).
58	The partition is demonstrated for this seven-feature set; alternative features (e.g., syntactic complexity, n-gram frequencies) may yield different groupings, though the convergence of five independent effect-size metrics suggests the location/shape asymmetry reflects distributional structure rather than feature-selection artifact.

61	\centering
62	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
63	\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. 64	\label{fig:feature-drift}
65	\end{figure}

67	Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
68	drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
69	while shape features remain near-stationary (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
70	The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and near-stationary features ($|\rho| < 0.10$) defines the DDR partition, with entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) as the sole intermediate member.
71	The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$; data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
72	
73	\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}
74	Two-sample KS tests confirm the split: drifting-feature statistics (0.516--0.537) are ${\sim}10\times$ larger than shape-feature statistics (0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$ after Bonferroni correction).
75	Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} (pooled, class-balanced) converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects (entropy mean $d{=}1.17$, TTR $d{=}0.88$, hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), while shape features are near zero (entropy max $d{=}0.08$, tail decay $d{=}0.08$).
76	Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); Glass's $\Delta$ (using gen-1 SD) amplifies drifting effects (entropy mean $\Delta{=}1.41$, hapax $\Delta{=}0.94$) while near-stationary features remain negligible ($\Delta \leq 0.10$), yielding a ${\geq}9.5\times$ gap. Cliff's $\delta$ corroborates the partition (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
77	Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
78	Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
79	Entropy min exhibits a discrepancy between location-based (Cohen's $d$\,=\,0.016) and rank-based (Cliff's $\delta$\,=\,0.354) effect sizes, indicating distributional shape change without location shift: recursive generation produces more extreme minimum-entropy tokens while preserving the mean. The near-stationary label refers specifically to location stability; rank-order sensitivity is documented in Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}.
80	The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
81	Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact; holdout generator validation confirms stability across two 4/4 splits (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
82	Bootstrap resampling (1{,}000 iterations) confirms these equivalence conclusions are robust: all three near-stationary features achieve 100\% rejection rate, with effect-size CIs well within the $d{=}0.20$ margin (Appendix~\ref{app:tost-bootstrap}).
83	Tail decay shows generator-dependent variation ($d{=}0.15$--$0.22$), but reclassifying it as intermediate preserves the core split and classification performance.
84	
85	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
86	The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
87	Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
88	PCA confirms the three drifting features share a single latent dimension (92.3\% variance, loadings 0.56--0.59; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}); replacing them with PC1 costs only 1.1\,pp binary F1, and retaining any single drifting feature with the four non-drifting features yields F1\,=\,0.692 (vs.\ 0.701 full).
89	DDR's contribution is identifying which distributional properties (NLL location vs.\ shape) are depth-sensitive; PC scores achieve equivalent classification but obscure which specific properties drift.
90	TTR and hapax ratio ($r = 0.97$) show permutation importance differences (0.35 vs.\ 0.18) due to feature masking \cite{strobl_conditional_2008}; all three are retained for marginal LOFO gains (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).
91	
92	\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
93	Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref} in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift.
94	Pythia generators' highest F1 (0.718--0.724) may partly reflect same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model, but the 0.013 cross-reference spread bounds this effect; depth features are robust to reference model choice, though this does not alone establish DDR as a fundamental property of recursive generation.
95	
96	\paragraph{Temperature and prompt-type sensitivity.}
97	The depth signal is modulated by decoding parameters and prompt type (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity},~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
98	All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is model-family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen).
99	Continuation chains show the strongest drift (binary F1\,=\,0.781), with cross-prompt-type transfer confirming shared signal (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753).
100	Per-feature convergence trajectories confirm this ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:convergence}); the DDR partition hierarchy is preserved across temperatures despite absolute effect-size compression (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).

Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B), with the primary difficulty being gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ discrimination (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).

A single-generator transfer analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:transfer}) provides evidence against this confound: classifiers trained on one generator transfer to all seven others with mean binary F1\,=\,0.810 (95\% CI [0.796, 0.822]), significantly above chance.

The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$; data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).

\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}
Two-sample KS tests confirm the split: drifting-feature statistics (0.516--0.537) are ${\sim}10\times$ larger than shape-feature statistics (0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$ after Bonferroni correction).
Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} (pooled, class-balanced) converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects (entropy mean $d{=}1.17$, TTR $d{=}0.88$, hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), while shape features are near zero (entropy max $d{=}0.08$, tail decay $d{=}0.08$).
Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); Glass's $\Delta$ (using gen-1 SD) amplifies drifting effects (entropy mean $\Delta{=}1.41$, hapax $\Delta{=}0.94$) while near-stationary features remain negligible ($\Delta \leq 0.10$), yielding a ${\geq}9.5\times$ gap. Cliff's $\delta$ corroborates the partition (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
Entropy min exhibits a discrepancy between location-based (Cohen's $d$\,=\,0.016) and rank-based (Cliff's $\delta$\,=\,0.354) effect sizes, indicating distributional shape change without location shift: recursive generation produces more extreme minimum-entropy tokens while preserving the mean. The near-stationary label refers specifically to location stability; rank-order sensitivity is documented in Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}.
The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact; holdout generator validation confirms stability across two 4/4 splits (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
Bootstrap resampling (1{,}000 iterations) confirms these equivalence conclusions are robust: all three near-stationary features achieve 100\% rejection rate, with effect-size CIs well within the $d{=}0.20$ margin (Appendix~\ref{app:tost-bootstrap}).
Tail decay shows generator-dependent variation ($d{=}0.15$--$0.22$), but reclassifying it as intermediate preserves the core split and classification performance.

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
PCA confirms the three drifting features share a single latent dimension (92.3\% variance, loadings 0.56--0.59; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}); replacing them with PC1 costs only 1.1\,pp binary F1, and retaining any single drifting feature with the four non-drifting features yields F1\,=\,0.692 (vs.\ 0.701 full).
DDR's contribution is identifying which distributional properties (NLL location vs.\ shape) are depth-sensitive; PC scores achieve equivalent classification but obscure which specific properties drift.
TTR and hapax ratio ($r = 0.97$) show permutation importance differences (0.35 vs.\ 0.18) due to feature masking \cite{strobl_conditional_2008}; all three are retained for marginal LOFO gains (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref} in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift.
Pythia generators' highest F1 (0.718--0.724) may partly reflect same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model, but the 0.013 cross-reference spread bounds this effect; depth features are robust to reference model choice, though this does not alone establish DDR as a fundamental property of recursive generation.

\paragraph{Temperature and prompt-type sensitivity.}
The depth signal is modulated by decoding parameters and prompt type (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity},~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is model-family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen).
Continuation chains show the strongest drift (binary F1\,=\,0.781), with cross-prompt-type transfer confirming shared signal (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753).
Per-feature convergence trajectories confirm this ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:convergence}); the DDR partition hierarchy is preserved across temperatures despite absolute effect-size compression (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

Do existing detection methods already capture depth signal?
To contextualize depth discrimination ability rather than claim competitive advantage, we repurpose four detection scores as ordinal depth predictors using the same XGBoost framework and LOGO splits (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

DDR's contribution is not classification performance but decomposing depth signal into location-sensitive and shape-stable components, a distinction absent from both binary detection methods and model collapse analyses (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
Permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention analyses confirm that DDR features carry causal predictive power beyond correlation: drifting features contribute $5.5\times$ more to classification than near-stationary ones, and 6/7 features exhibit significant Granger causality across generation depths, with entropy\_min as the sole exception (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).
This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow 1.0$: overall 3-class F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.723; the most affected single generator, Qwen3-1.7B, drops to per-generator F1\,=\,0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).

DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; inference-chain drift operates in a different regime where parameters are fixed, drift is fully reversible, and shape features are affected an order of magnitude less.
This divergence has practical implications: model collapse remediation focuses on restoring tail coverage, while inference-chain contamination preserves shape and thus requires location-based detection---a strategy that DDR directly enables.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), though richer representations recover substantially more signal (QLoRA F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
Instruction-tuned models show attenuated fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base), but QLoRA on instruct data (F1\,=\,0.89--0.91 vs.\ XGBoost 0.58--0.73; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}) indicates instruction tuning reorganizes rather than eliminates the signal, though this is demonstrated under within-model CV only; cross-generator instruct transfer (XGBoost LOGO F1\,=\,0.487) remains weak.

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).

Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.789, binary F1\,=\,0.830; evaluated on the 5-generator subset for which cross-model chains were available), though these generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.

\subsection{9-Generator Scale Evaluation}\label{app:9gen-scale}

This analysis extends the 8-generator LOGO evaluation to nine generators by adding Gemma-2-2B, a model from a previously unrepresented architecture family (Gemma).
All results use class-balanced LOGO; the 8-gen averages here (0.770/0.701) differ slightly from Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} (0.762/0.694), which uses an unfiltered protocol.
Table~\ref{tab:9gen-logo} reports per-generator LOGO performance under this expanded set.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{9-generator LOGO evaluation. Each row holds out the listed generator at test time. 3-class: gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. 95\% bootstrap CIs in brackets.}
\label{tab:9gen-logo}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llr cc cc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia  & 1.0B & 0.857 & [0.848, 0.866] & 0.785 & --- \\
Qwen3-0.6B      & Qwen    & 0.6B & 0.819 & [0.807, 0.830] & 0.743 & --- \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia  & 2.8B & 0.812 & [0.801, 0.822] & 0.728 & --- \\
Qwen3-1.7B      & Qwen    & 1.7B & 0.811 & [0.800, 0.823] & 0.746 & --- \\
OLMo-2-1B       & OLMo    & 1.5B & 0.773 & [0.762, 0.784] & 0.692 & --- \\
Llama-3.2-3B    & Llama   & 3.2B & 0.759 & [0.748, 0.770] & 0.680 & --- \\
Qwen3-8B        & Qwen    & 8.2B & 0.696 & [0.683, 0.709] & 0.647 & [0.631, 0.664] \\
Gemma-2-2B      & Gemma   & 2.6B & 0.628 & [0.622, 0.634] & 0.440 & [0.432, 0.449] \\
Mistral-7B      & Mistral & 7.0B & 0.605 & [0.593, 0.617] & 0.534 & --- \\
\midrule
\textbf{Average (9-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.751} & & \textbf{0.666} & \\
\textbf{Average (8-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.770} & & \textbf{0.701} & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Overall comparison.}
Adding Gemma-2-2B reduces the mean 3-class LOGO F1 from 0.770 (8-gen) to 0.751 (9-gen), a drop of $\Delta = -0.019$.
The per-generator F1 values for the original eight generators shift by at most $[-0.011, +0.002]$, indicating that the inclusion of Gemma data in training does not destabilize existing generalization patterns.

\paragraph{Gemma-2-2B anomaly.}
Gemma-2-2B is the weakest held-out generator: 3-class F1\,=\,0.628, binary F1\,=\,0.440.
Per-class breakdown reveals a striking asymmetry: gen-0 F1\,=\,0.991 and gen-2+ F1\,=\,0.856, but gen-1 F1\,=\,0.036---the classifier almost entirely fails to identify first-generation Gemma continuations.
This is not a data-quality artifact: the Gemma-2-2B partition contains 4{,}957 instances with a balanced depth distribution ($\sim$990 per level).
A plausible explanation is that Gemma-2's first-generation continuations occupy a region of feature space highly similar to human-written text (gen-0), causing systematic misclassification of gen-1 as gen-0 or gen-2+.
This constitutes an architecture-specific generalization limitation rather than a systemic failure of the depth fingerprinting approach.

\paragraph{Scale effect.}
A clear parameter-count gradient emerges across the nine generators: three of four sub-1.7B generators achieve F1\,$>$\,0.81 (OLMo-2-1B at 0.773 is the exception), mid-range models (2--3B) cluster at 0.63--0.81, and large models (7B+) fall to 0.60--0.70.
Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters) achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.696 under the 9-gen split, compared to 0.701 in the class-balanced 8-gen evaluation; this small difference reflects the changed training composition rather than a property of the Qwen3-8B generator itself.
